query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin, approximately 5–10 μm 2D high-entropy sulfide triboactive coating (e.g., a (MoWNbTaV)xS2-like layer) on the surface of a high-entropy alloy will promote in situ tribochemical reactions that form a lubricious, self-renewing tribofilm during sliding, thereby reducing both the friction coefficient and wear rate relative to the untreated alloy across a broad service-temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: An untreated high-entropy alloy intended for self-lubricating moving components.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin, 2D high-entropy alloy-based triboactive coating containing sulfide components using surface/interface engineering techniques.
generation.conditions: Dynamic sliding conditions under a wide temperature range (from near ambient to high temperatures) and under cyclic loading typical of moving component applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an in situ, self-renewing tribofilm mediated by sulfide and oxide phases (e.g., MoO2-like regions) at the interface.
generation.mechanism: The engineered coating promotes tribocatalytic reactions during sliding exposure that generate a lubricious tribofilm. This film reduces direct metal-to-metal contact, mitigates adhesive and abrasive wear, and accommodates temperature-induced variations in surface chemistry through controlled oxidation/sulfidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated high-entropy alloy will exhibit a lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate compared to the untreated alloy, with sustained performance over a wide temperature range.
generation.baseline: The untreated high-entropy alloy without any surface modification.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to remain effective under typical service loads and gradual temperature variations; however, extremely high loads or excessively rapid temperature cycling may exceed the tribofilm’s renewal capacity, potentially compromising performance.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term durability of the triboactive coating under extended cyclic loading and extreme environmental fluctuations is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of high-entropy alloy specimens with the deposited 2D high-entropy sulfide triboactive coating and one set of untreated specimens. Subject both sets to sliding wear tests under controlled normal loads and sliding speeds across a wide temperature range (e.g., room temperature, intermediate, and elevated temperatures). Monitor the evolution of friction and wear over a series of cycles.
measurements: Real-time friction coefficient measurement using a tribometer
Quantitative wear rate determination via profilometry of wear tracks
Surface chemical analysis (e.g., XPS, SEM) of the wear tracks to detect tribofilm formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If at any measured temperature the coated samples do not consistently show a statistically significant decrease in both friction coefficient and wear rate relative to the untreated samples, or if the intended in situ tribofilm does not form during sliding, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

decision.trend: Early work (PMC7311485, 2020) showed that high-entropy alloys can achieve surprisingly low friction and wear via near-surface dynamic amorphization under vacuum settings. Subsequently, efforts turned to composite approaches (PMC8949536, 2022) by adding WC reinforcements to AlCoCrFeNi and to dual-phase microstructures (PMC9571794, 2022) to raise base hardness and wear resistance. More recent studies used nanohierarchical designs to trigger adaptive friction interfaces that function across a broader temperature range (PMC10241162, 2023) and examined amorphous-structured high-entropy alloy films for enhanced oxidation control and tribocorrosion resistance at elevated temperatures (PMC10456374, 2023). Finally, research on 2D high-entropy alloy nanoflakes (PMC12019924, 2025) revealed that tribo-catalytic self-lubrication can aggressively lower friction and wear by unleashing in situ lubrication under high loads and in ambient conditions.
decision.unsolved: Despite these advances, there is still a need to sustain low friction and long-lasting wear resistance over a wide temperature spectrum without resorting solely to composition changes. Achieving robust, self-adapting tribofilms and stable lubrication from low to high temperatures remains a challenge, especially while avoiding undesired oxidation or brittleness at elevated temperatures and friction-induced damage at ambient conditions.
decision.lever: Deposit a thin, 2D high-entropy alloy-based triboactive coating (e.g., a (MoWNbTaV)xS2-like layer) to induce in situ tribochemical reactions for lubrication across a broad temperature range, with controlled thickness (~5–10 μm) to ensure durability under cyclic loading.
decision.why: Building on the trend of 2D-based self-lubricating approaches and the success of adaptive tribofilms in wide-temperature applications, a specialized 2D ‘high-entropy-sulfide’ coating can be engineered to form and continuously renew boundary films under dynamic sliding, reducing friction and wear. This lever addresses the persistent challenge of achieving stable, broad-range temperature performance and extends prior findings about tribo-catalytic lubrication mechanisms in HEAs.
